newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar gains seen limited in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains seen limited in Asia.

text.p: The dollar's topside is likely to be capped against the yen and the mark in Asia on Wednesday and overall activity is expected to be subdued ahead of a Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting later in the day.
Japanese exporters are expected to sell dollars steadily above 115.00 yen, making it difficult to break through 115.50 yen, while the downside could be supported by investor bids.
"Steady selling by Japanese exporters is expected when the dollar rises above 115.00 yen," said a Japanese bank dealer.
"It will probably take few days to absorb such offers placed between 115.00-115.50 yen," she added.
The bank dealer said, however, that some technical charts had started suggesting a bull trend for the dollar.

On the downside, a lack of conspicuous dollar selling factors and talk of bids by Japanese investors could support the dollar, with an initial support point seen at 114.50 yen and then at around 114.30 yen.

A dealer at a trust bank said there was talk of bids by a Japanese public investment body at around 114.30 yen and below 114.00 yen. "There are operators keen to pick up the dollar on falls," he added. Further falls in the Tokyo stock market could also give a support to the dollar/yen rate, dealers said.
The trust bank dealer said the dollar could find it difficult to reach a tough resistance of 1.7500 marks in Asia although the point was said to be a "trigger point" for knockout-option positions.
Should that point be broken, stop-loss dollar buying related to these options positions is expected.

But sterling's falls against the mark overnight, prompted by uncertainty over the U.K. budget on Wednesday and weak U.K. purchasing managers' index data on Tuesday, put downward pressure on the dollar against the mark.
In New York, the dollar was sustained by remarks by Bundesbank President Tietmeyer and U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.

Tietmeyer, speaking in Frankfurt on Tuesday, said he preferred to think of the dollar as strong rather than the mark as weak, while Summers said he believed the dollar was "in a very strong position".
